title: Predictable Inference Contract Playbook for Platform Ops
body:
Purpose: quick reference playbook for commercial + platform engineering when negotiating Reserved/Isolated inference contracts with enterprise buyers. Focus: make offers procurement-ready — clear guarantees, measurable acceptance criteria, and defensible fallbacks that protect both customer uptime and Redwood economics.

Elevator pitch (one-liner for procurement decks):
We provide dedicated inference pools with SLA-backed throughput and isolation, clear latency and capacity SLOs, and standardized onboarding milestones so platform teams can predict cost and performance without building their own serving stack.

Buyer personas & primary concerns:
- Platform/Infra Leads: want predictable per-hour throughput, isolation guarantees, and clear failure modes + remediation latency.
- Product/ML Engineering: need stable P99 latency for interactive features and consistent token throughput for batch workloads.
- Procurement/Finance: wants simple billing cadence, termination/exit terms, and risk transfer clauses.
- Security/Compliance: requires VPC/private control plane options and KMS/HSM integration.

Core guarantees we recommend offering (contract language to adapt):
- Throughput guarantee: committed throughput expressed as tokens/sec or requests/sec (e.g., 200M tokens/day, or X requests/min at Y concurrency). Measured weekly, 95% of weeks must meet >= committed throughput.
- Latency SLOs: p50/p95/p99 for typical request types (short chat turn vs long generation) tied to defined payload sizes. Example: p95 < 150ms for short-turn (<= 128 tokens), p99 < 800ms for long-turn (<= 1024 tokens).
- Isolation: dedicated GPU pools with tenant-level network isolation; noisy-neighbor mitigation clause; guaranteed compute capacity reserved for customer per region.
- Availability: SLA-backed uptime for control plane and inference endpoints (example: 99.5% inference availability per month for dedicated capacity).
- Data handling & keys: KMS-backed key control, optional on-prem bundle for air-gapped deployments.

Operational acceptance criteria (onboarding milestones):
- Week 0–2: Provisioning and VPC peering, initial capacity allocation verified by perf test.
- Week 2–4: Baseline perf test with customer's representative workloads (scripts provided by Redwood); pass defined throughput and latency thresholds.
- Week 4–6: Canary traffic (10–25% of production) and rollout plan sign-off.
- Post-launch (30 days): SLA goes live once run-rate and synthetic checks are green for 7 consecutive days.

Procurement-friendly clauses (short, plain-language fragments to hand to legal):
- Scope of Services: "Redwood will provide dedicated inference capacity as described in Appendix A (capacity and region list)."
- Performance Credits: "Missed monthly availability or SLOs accrue service credits up to X% of monthly fee; credits limited to Y months of fees."
- Failure Modes & Escalation: "Runbook steps and 24/7 on-call contact for P1 incidents; initial acknowledgement within 15 minutes, remediation ETA depending on incident class."
- Data & Termination: "Upon contract termination, customer data snapshots and KV caches will be retained for 30 days for orderly migration unless otherwise requested."

Negotiation levers and seller responses (talking points for AE + solutions engineer):
- Customer: "We need 100% isolation and instant autoscale."
  - Redwood: "We offer tenant-dedicated pools and predictable reserved capacity; autoscale is configurable with burst buckets and warm pools to balance cost and instant scale. For instant scale guarantees we recommend a short warm-up window tied to burst capacity add-on."
- Customer: "We can't accept service credits as sole remedy."
  - Redwood: "We can include joint runbook commitments and an optional enhanced SLAs bundle (extended credits + technical playbook with monthly operational reviews)."
- Customer: "We need price certainty for 3 years."
  - Redwood: "We provide annual pricing with optional multi-year committed discounts; hardware refresh costs are flagged 90 days ahead with protection clauses for major revisions."

Competitive positioning vs common alternatives (bullet takeaways):
- Self-hosted on cloud VMs: cheaper sticker in some cases but high operational risk and hidden cost (engineer hours + tuning). Sell: predictable cost model, faster time-to-prod, and SRE-grade observability.
- Managed single-tenant vendors: similar isolation but lower transparency or no developer-first API. Sell: Redwood’s unified API + runtime+ console + rollout tooling reduces app-level risk and regression surface.
- Hyperscaler-hosted model endpoints: broad coverage but limited model catalog and inconsistent latency across regions. Sell: predictable per-route latency and model variant fallbacks optimized for cost/latency tradeoffs.

Pricing framing for procurement decks (simple):
- Commitment tiering: baseline reserved capacity (monthly commit) + optional burst bucket (pay-as-you-go for overflow).
- Unit economics: show $/M tokens at committed rates vs on-demand; emphasize predictable monthly spend and lower TCO when accounting for ops.

Short technical appendix (copyable bullets to attach to SOW):
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100/V100 family (specify region-specific GPU SKUs); reserved GPU ratio and overprovisioning tolerance.
- Observability: token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency histograms, per-request trace IDs and sample outputs for regressions.
- Model compatibility: list supported model families and recommended quantization profiles; automatic fallback to compatible variant on capacity constraints.

Common procurement questions (with suggested answers):
- "How do you measure throughput?" -> "Measured at ingress tokens/sec with standard client SDK counters; Redwood will run joint perf tests during onboarding."
- "What does isolation mean?" -> "Logical tenant isolation combined with dedicated GPU pools; network isolation options available via VPC."
- "How to escape vendor lock-in?" -> "Customers can pin model versions and export KV caches and snapshots; migration support included in enterprise tier."

Quick checklist for AE before sending to procurement/legal:
- Confirm region(s) and GPU SKUs required.
- Define committed throughput units and latency SLOs in plain language.
- Choose availability SLA and corresponding credit cap.
- Attach onboarding perf-test plan and runbook.

Appendix: sample KPIs to include in monthly reviews
- Average token throughput vs committed (%), p99 latency for primary routes, number of incidents impacting committed capacity, cost per 1M tokens compared to baseline.

Notes / open questions for product/legal:
- Standardize a "burst add-on" pricing SKU for instant scale guarantees.
- Draft minimal legal language for KMS/HSM handling and retained logs for audits.
- Confirm template for per-region GPU SKU listing (Appendix A).

End — use this as a working checklist to tailor customer-facing SOWs. Keep it simple in procurement docs; preserve technical detail in attached appendix runbook.
